title: A continent of plastic
text: Between Hawaii and California, ocean currents {{1}} a region twice the size of France where the water is calmer than the sea around it — and quieter seas collect floating rubbish. The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is not an island of bottles you could walk on; most of it is a {{2}} of confetti-sized fragments suspended through the top metres of water, with fishing nets and floats accounting for most of the {{3}}. The fragments matter more than their size suggests: sunlight and waves {{4}} plastic into ever smaller pieces, small enough for plankton-feeding animals to {{5}} with their food. Samples from the patch contain more plastic than living plankton by weight in places, and the chemical additives in plastic {{6}} into the tissues of whatever swallows them. Cleanup technology {{7}} — floating barriers that concentrate the debris for removal — but researchers keep {{8}} the same point: the only real cleanup happens on land, where roughly eighty per cent of ocean plastic begins its journey. Rivers, not ships, deliver most of it; intercept the rivers and the patch slowly starves.

gaps.explanation: 'currents trap a region of calm water' — hold debris in it; wrap = cover, scrap = discard.
'most of it is a haze of confetti-sized fragments' — a thin, diffuse cloud; a handful is far too small a scale, and haste and hammer do not take this pattern.
'accounting for most of the mass' — the bulk of the weight; mast = a ship's pole, moss = a small green plant.
'waves break plastic into ever smaller pieces' — split it; brake = stop, brood = dwell gloomily.
'small enough to swallow with their food' — take in; waddle = walk like a duck, wallow = roll about in mud.
'additives leach into the tissues' — drain out of the plastic; leash = put a dog on a lead, latch = fasten a door.
'cleanup technology exists' — is available; insist takes 'on', desist takes 'from', consist takes 'of'.
'keep making the same point' — 'make a point' is the fixed phrase; mask = hide.
